turns.prompt: Which port does the load balancer use for the gateway's health check, and how do I roll out a new build?
turns.reply:
The load balancer reads the gateway's health check on port 8080; HTTPS traffic stays on 8443 (Projects/harbor-gateway/Gateway ports.md).

To roll out a new build (Projects/harbor-gateway/Deploying the gateway.md):

1. Build the image with `make image`.
2. Push it with `make push TAG=2.3.1`.
3. Run `deployctl rollout harbor-gateway --zone a`, then zones b and c, and wait for the health check in each zone before the next.

A rollout that fails its health check rolls back by itself.

turns.prompt: Can I run the entries schema migration on the first of the month?
turns.reply:
Not on the first. The month-end close runs on the first working day of each month, and until Finance signs off (by noon) there are no migrations and no deploys (Projects/tide-ledger/Month-end close.md).

This one also locks the entries table, so it goes out on a weekend, announced in #ledger a week ahead (Projects/tide-ledger/Schema migrations.md).

turns.prompt: Remember the keepalive gotcha for the harbor gateway: the load balancer drops idle connections after 60 seconds.

args.title: Gateway keepalive
args.body:
Set the harbor gateway's upstream keepalive to 30 seconds. The load balancer drops idle connections after 60 seconds, so a longer keepalive ends in connection resets.

## How we found it

Clients behind the load balancer saw resets every few minutes; the gateway logs showed each one 60 seconds after the last byte. With the keepalive at 30 seconds they stopped.

turns.prompt: Clients behind the load balancer see connection resets every few minutes. Find out why.
turns.reply:
The load balancer drops idle connections after 60 seconds, but the gateway keeps idle upstream connections open longer than that. The next request on such a connection gets a reset.

Setting the upstream keepalive to 30 seconds in `gateway.toml` stops the resets: the gateway now closes an idle connection before the load balancer does.

turns.prompt: Should the rate limiter refill each bucket on a timer, or when a request comes in?
turns.think: A timer touches every bucket on each tick, also the idle ones. The gateway has about 40,000 client buckets, and most of them get no traffic in a given second, so that is 40,000 writes a second for nothing. A refill on request: tokens = min(burst, tokens + rate × elapsed), then take one. That is one clock read for each request and no work in the background. The result does not depend on a tick length. One edge case: the clock can go back (an NTP step), so the elapsed time can be negative. Clamp it at zero. src/limits.js already has this for /api/orders.
turns.reply:
Refill when a request comes in. Each bucket keeps its token count and the time of its last refill; a request adds `rate × elapsed` tokens, up to the burst, and then takes one.

- **No work for idle clients.** A timer would touch all 40,000 buckets on each tick, and most of them get no traffic.
- **Exact at any rate.** The refill comes from the elapsed time, so it does not depend on a tick length.
- **One edge case.** When the clock goes back, the elapsed time is negative: clamp it at zero.

`src/limits.js` already does this for `/api/orders`, so the other routes can use the same function.
